Circumcision (Sign)
sur-kum-SIZ-yun SYNE
noun phrase (biblical-theological concept)
From Latin circumcisio (a cutting around, from circumcidere, from circum, around, + caedere, to cut) + Latin signum (sign, mark, token, seal). The Hebrew berit milah (the covenant of cutting, milah from mul, to circumcise) and the Greek peritomē (circumcision, from peri, around, + temnein, to cut) denote the rite, while sēmeion (sign, token, mark confirming a truth) designates its covenantal function as Paul expounds it in Romans 4:11.

Biblical Definition

Circumcision as a covenant sign was instituted by God in Genesis 17 as the outward seal of the Abrahamic covenant: “And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.” (Gen 17:11). Paul's exposition in Romans 4:11 is definitive: Abraham “received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while uncircumcised” — circumcision did not cause Abraham's justification (which preceded it by 14-plus years according to Gen 15–17) but sealed and confirmed it. The sign pointed inward to the true circumcision of the heart (Deut 10:16; Jer 4:4; Col 2:11) — the cutting away of the old man, the carnal nature, the uncircumcised heart that cannot receive God's covenant. In the New Testament, Paul argues that circumcision in the flesh neither adds anything to the justified Gentile nor removes anything from the justified Jew, because the reality it pointed to — the putting off of the body of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ (Col 2:11) — has arrived in the death and resurrection of Jesus. Christ's cross is the true circumcision: the flesh cut off in his substitutionary death, the new man made alive in his resurrection. The New Testament sign corresponding to Old Testament circumcision is baptism (Col 2:11–12), where “buried with him in baptism” translates the circumcision-metaphor into the water-rite of the new covenant. Reformed covenant theology (the Westminster Confession, 28.1; the 1689 Confession, 29.1) grounds infant baptism in the continuity between circumcision and baptism as the covenant-entry signs of the respective administrations of the one covenant of grace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Circumcision as the divinely instituted outward sign and seal of the Abrahamic covenant (Gen 17:11) — pointing inward to the true circumcision of the heart, fulfilled in Christ's cross as the true cutting-off of the flesh, and succeeded in the new covenant by baptism as the corresponding covenant-entry rite.

expand to see more

CIRCUMCISION (sign), n. The rite of cutting away the male foreskin as God's appointed outward sign and seal of the covenant of grace in its Abrahamic administration (Gen 17:11); distinguished here from the bodily rite itself by its covenantal-sign function.

2. PAUL'S DEFINITION (Rom 4:11): “he received the sign of circumcision — a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while uncircumcised” — circumcision as sēmeion (sign, token of a reality it does not produce) and sphragis (seal, authentication of a reality already present).

3. INWARD REFERENT (Deut 10:16; Jer 4:4; Col 2:11): the outward sign pointed to the circumcision of the heart — the cutting away of the old nature's dominion — which only God can perform (Deut 30:6) and which is accomplished in the believer's union with Christ in his death.

4. FULFILLMENT IN CHRIST (Col 2:11–12): “you were circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands — by the putting off of the body of the flesh — by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism” — the cross is the true circumcision, baptism its new-covenant sign.

5. REFORMED ARGUMENT: Paedobaptism rests on the circumcision-baptism continuity (Col 2:11–12) — both signs mark covenant-entry, both point to the same inward reality (regeneration), and the new-covenant administration replaces the old sign with baptism without abolishing the covenantal pattern of signing children of the covenant.

Key Scripture

Gen 17:11 — "And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you."

Rom 4:11 — "And he received the sign of circumcision — a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while uncircumcised — so that he might be the father of all who believe without being circumcised, that righteousness might be credited to them,"

Col 2:11 — "In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ:"

Deut 10:16 — "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked."

Modern Corruption

Circumcision as a covenant sign has been distorted in two directions: by those who attach saving virtue to the physical rite itself (the Judaizer error Paul combats in Galatians), and by those who so sever the old and new covenants that they deny any covenantal continuity between circumcision and baptism.

expand to see more

The Judaizer error of Galatia (Gal 5:2–4) attached salvific necessity to physical circumcision: “if you receive circumcision, Christ will be of no benefit to you.” Paul's response is not to deny the sign's validity within its proper redemptive-historical context but to insist that the arrival of the reality (justification by faith in Christ) has made the old sign an obstacle when imposed as a condition of salvation. In the new covenant, circumcision is neither required (Gal 5:6: “in Christ Jesus, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything, but faith working through love”) nor prohibited; it is simply irrelevant to standing before God. Attaching salvific weight to any outward rite — circumcision, water baptism, confirmation — when the reality has arrived is the perennial form of the Judaizer error.

On the other side, hyper-dispensationalism so severs the Testaments that it denies any typological continuity between circumcision and baptism, treating Col 2:11–12 as referring to spiritual circumcision only and denying any connection to water baptism. But the passage's syntax connects the circumcision-of-Christ directly to burial-in-baptism: “having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him” (v. 12) — the water-rite is the new-covenant counterpart to the old-covenant cutting, functioning as the sign of the same underlying spiritual reality: the putting off of the old man and the putting on of the new.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew milah (circumcision, cutting) and its covenantal formula berit milah (covenant of cutting) ground the rite in the Abrahamic covenant-ratification vocabulary, with the Greek sēmeion (sign) and sphragis (seal) defining its New Testament theological function.

expand to see more

Hebrew mul — to circumcise, cut around; the verb of the covenant rite commanded in Gen 17; its passive-resultive milah names the rite itself

Hebrew berit milah — the covenant of cutting; the rabbinic name for the Abrahamic covenant-sign, which connects its cutting-metaphor to the “cutting a covenant” (karat berit) formula of Genesis

Greek sēmeion — sign, token; Paul's term in Rom 4:11 for circumcision's function — it points to a reality beyond itself (Abraham's justifying faith), which it confirms without causing

Greek sphragis — seal, stamp of authentication; Paul's second term in Rom 4:11 — circumcision authenticated the righteousness Abraham already possessed by faith, sealing it in his flesh

Greek peritomē — circumcision; in Col 2:11, Paul redefines the term christologically: the real peritomē is Christ's death, which cuts off the body of flesh and is signed in baptism

Usage

"Philippians 3:3 — “we are the true circumcision, who worship in the Spirit of God, and glory in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in the flesh” — identifies the true covenant people not by physical rite but by Spirit-worship, Christ-glorying, and flesh-renouncing faith: the inward reality the sign always pointed to."

"The rite's connection to the eighth-day requirement (Gen 17:12; Lev 12:3; Luke 2:21) has been typologically read as pointing to the “eighth day” of new creation — the day beyond the old Sabbath-cycle, which is Sunday, the day of resurrection, when the new-covenant sign (baptism) is also appropriately administered."

"In the Patristic period, Chrysostom and Augustine both used the circumcision-baptism parallel to argue for the legitimacy of infant participation in the covenant community: as infant males received the covenant sign under the Abrahamic administration, so infant children of believers receive the covenant sign under the new administration."
